P = NP basically just says that every question whose solution can be verified quickly can also be solved quickly.
Of course, it is overwhelmingly likely that P != NP, meaning that there are some questions that are easier to verify than solve.

For example, if you had to find two prime numbers that when multiplied together make 90113, it would be very difficult. But it is easy to verify that 929 and 97 do indeed multiply to equal 90113.

But P != NP has not been formally proven in mathematics. The reason that P != NP has not been proven is that is difficult to prove that there can be no possible counterexample to P != NP. It's like trying to disprove the existence of unicorns.

If P = NP were to be true, it would be an insane turn of events and would directly impact many things. Most relevant to this board, bitcoin relies entirely on cryptographic methods to function and would be worthless if P = NP. It would impact a lot of banking and finance as well.

62949809
>>62949785
Some good ideas Anon but to add some feedback:
Your opening description is basically right, and 929 x 97 = 90,113 is a good example of how easy it can be to check someone’s answer. One subtlety: even if P ≠ NP, factoring could still have a polynomial-time algorithm. P ≠ NP would tell us that some problems are harder to solve than to verify. It wouldn’t tell us that factoring is one of them.

The unicorn analogy also needs more context. To prove P ≠ NP, you wouldn’t have to test every possible algorithm. It would be enough to find a mathematical reason why any algorithm that correctly solves SAT must take more than polynomial time in the worst case. Finding that reason is the hard part.

Also, "Bitcoin would be worthless.” Bitcoin uses elliptic-curve signatures, so faster factoring alone wouldn’t break them. And even if someone proved P = NP, an algorithm taking n^100 steps would count as polynomial while being hopelessly slow in practice. If someone could cheaply forge Bitcoin signatures at the key sizes people actually use, that would be a serious threat. That’s a stronger claim than P = NP, and predicting Bitcoin’s price would require another argument.

>If a human proved P ≠ NP tomorrow, would you say it achieved none of the good of a proof because it delivered no faster algorithm?
By itself? Of course not.
>is P = NP?
>yep/nope
What changes? Nothing. The assumption is that the process of arriving at the proof leads to new discoveries which change our fundamental mathematical capabilities, not that the answer itself is relevant. Sure, knowing it is good I guess, but ESPECIALLY a negative result really contributes very little, at least separated from the attendant knowledge gained from arriving at the proof.

This is true of most “theoretical math”. The value is not the answers to these questions but the tools used to arrive at them.

Incidentally, this is veering away from my broader point. My point is that the biggest question for AI is not “what can it do?” but rather “why have an AI do it?” Nobody cares what it CAN do if that’s not worthwhile. In the domain of “tasks humans are already doing” there are major accountability and, beyond that, cost concerns that Anthropic is nowhere near solving, which makes their path to profitability shaky.

WRT frontier math, you can kind of end-run that argument by saying “well if it’s doing things humans CAN’T do at all, who’s to say it’s not cost effective?” and my point is, it doing those things is not meaningful unless we get the positive side effects we get from humans doing them (greater understanding of math as a whole) so again: why have an AI do it?

Stop asking whether it can, start asking whether it should.

That doesn't mean we'd be flying to alpha centuari any time soon. The proof would just be an incomprehensible fact that would couldn't make any use of.

62949082
>>62949009
Suppose two researchers are working on SAT. One wants an algorithm guaranteed to solve every instance in polynomial time. The other wants an algorithm that runs quickly on the particular instances their factory encounters. If P ≠ NP were proved tomorrow, the first researcher would know their specification is impossible. The second would still have every reason to continue. Both could act on that information without borrowing a single technique from the proof. That’s what changes: we learn which promise an engineer can reasonably be asked to deliver.
And “we already suspected that” doesn’t erase the difference. Before the proof, every failed attempt leaves two possibilities open: maybe this approach failed, or maybe every approach must fail. A negative theorem can settle which explanation is right. That’s a substantial piece of knowledge about the problem itself.

>Incidentally, this is veering away from my broader point. My point is that the biggest question for AI is not “what can it do?” but rather “why have an AI do it?” Nobody cares what it CAN do if that’s not worthwhile.
Suppose a mathematician is about to spend a month trying to prove a conjecture. An AI finds a counterexample overnight, and the mathematician verifies it in ten minutes. Why have an AI do it? Because the mathematician can spend that month investigating why the conjecture fails instead of trying to prove something false. The counterexample has the same mathematical value whoever finds it. Getting it sooner has additional value.
Now change one detail. Suppose the AI produces so many plausible but incorrect counterexamples that checking them takes longer than doing the original work. What changes is its demonstrated performance, including the cost of checking it.

>Stop asking whether it can, start asking whether it should.
Why stop? We can ask both. My point was that AI can contribute to mathematical research.

62949166
>>62949082
>The second would still have every reason to continue. Both could act on that information without borrowing a single technique from the proof.
But in practical terms that’s nonsense. Inagine a solution that’s disputably either nlog(n) (NP) or 300,000*N (P) for a problem with at most 3,000 simultaneous inputs? Whether a problem is worth optimizing in real world terms is contextual. Just knowing P=NP by itself means shit. What are the bounds? Sure if there’s a transform that takes, say, n^k to 2kn steps it’s universally valuable but again that assumes a lot of knowledge beyond the problem statement of P=NP

62949181

62949190
>>62949166
Yes, real-world optimization is contextual. That was exactly my point about the second researcher. If a factory only handles inputs up to size 3,000, its engineer should test which algorithm works best on those inputs. A proof of P ≠ NP would still leave that work worth doing. What it would settle is the first researcher’s question: can one algorithm solve every SAT instance in polynomial time? You’ve switched from my hypothetical P ≠ NP to P = NP, and from a guarantee for all input sizes to performance on one bounded workload. Those are different questions.

There’s also a technical error in your example. Both n log n and 300,000n are polynomial-time bounds. An n log n runtime qualifies because it grows more slowly than n^2. For decision problems, either bound puts the problem in P, and every problem in P is also in NP. If you mean those expressions as exact step counts, your practical point is right: at n=3,000, log_2 n is about 34,650 steps, while 300,000n is 900 million. That illustrates how much performance can vary within P.

If we take your P = NP hypothetical instead, I agree we’d still need the actual runtime before recommending an algorithm to a factory. But “this theorem doesn’t tell me which software to buy” is a much narrower claim than “this theorem tells us nothing.” The theorem settles what is possible in principle. The benchmark settles what is worth running at the factory.

Ceded, I didn’t realize it had to be quadratic at minimum to qualify as non-polynomial.

I guess my point is more something like the heat equation. An unsolved problem where the solution was inventing the Fourier Transform, which revolutionized our understanding of acoustics and optics, and laid the groundwork for electrical engineering and signal processing. It can also function as a heat equation… but nobody cares. Our need for a deterministic heat equation were minimal, and if you DO need to predict the thermal evolution of a system, it’s easier and good enough to run a simulation.

The real benefit was all the shit we learned from the process of solving something unsolved. If we could have asked Claude “how will this thermal system evolve” and get an accurate answer, what would it have mattered? It’d be more expensive to generate than a simulation and we wouldn’t have learned the Fourier Transform

62949392
>>62949262
I would agree that if I want tomorrow’s temperature at one point in a metal rod, and an existing simulation gives me an accurate answer more cheaply, I should use the simulation. But Fourier was asking a broader question. Give Claude that same question: “For a rod with fixed end temperatures, derive a rule for how any initial temperature pattern evolves, and show why the rule works.” That’s a fair comparison.
The distinction matters even if we only care about heat. Fourier’s solution tells us that a temperature pattern with half the wavelength decays at four times the rate. In plain English, closely spaced hot and cold patches even out faster than broad ones, and we can say exactly how much faster. That’s something you can understand, reuse, and use to check a simulation. If an AI derived that relationship and supplied reasoning people could verify, what part of that knowledge would be unavailable to us because of who derived it?
I’d even grant your strongest point: if everyone had accepted a temperature prediction and stopped asking why, they might have missed a major discovery. But that would also be true if they’d accepted the output of your preferred simulation and stopped there. That’s a reason to keep asking for explanations. It doesn’t establish that involving AI prevents us from finding them.

Also, one small correction: quadratic time, n^2, is still polynomial time. So are n^3 and even n^100. There’s no cutoff at quadratic. An example of superpolynomial growth is 2^n, which eventually grows faster than every fixed power of n.
Your practical point still stands: calling an algorithm “polynomial-time” tells us something about how it's runtime scales. Whether it’s fast enough for a factory handling 3,000 inputs is a separate question.
